intro: This branch looks at how whole numbers are built from other numbers: factors (numbers that divide in exactly) and multiples (the numbers in a times table). These ideas are the tools for simplifying and adding fractions later on.

II.4.01.what: Finding factor pairs: two whole numbers that multiply to make a given number, like 6 and 7 for 42.

levels.a: Finds a factor pair of a small number, such as 2 and 4 for 8.
levels.b: Reads a factor pair from the rows and columns of an array.
levels.c: Finds all the factor pairs of numbers up to 50, spotting any that are missing.
levels.d: The same for numbers up to 100.

II.4.02.what: Understanding multiples: the numbers you land on when counting in steps of a given number, like 3, 6, 9, 12.

levels.a: Continues a list of multiples by counting in steps.
levels.b: Decides whether a number is a multiple of another.
levels.c: Predicts which squares on a hundred chart will be shaded for a given times table.
levels.d: Sees that if 5 times 7 is 35, then 35 is a multiple of 5 and 5 is a factor of 35.

II.4.03.what: Sorting numbers into primes, which have exactly two factors (1 and themselves), and composites, which have more.

levels.a: Uses a list of factors to decide whether a number is prime or composite.
levels.b: Recognizes the prime numbers up to 20.
levels.c: Recognizes the prime numbers up to 100.
levels.d: Explains why 1 is neither prime nor composite: it has only one factor.

II.4.04.what: Finding all the primes up to 100 with an ancient method: crossing out the multiples of each prime on a number chart.

levels.a: Crosses out the multiples of 2, keeping 2 itself.
levels.b: Then crosses out the multiples of 3 and of 5.
levels.c: Then crosses out the multiples of 7.
levels.d: Understands that the numbers left over are exactly the primes.

II.4.05.what: Breaking a number down into the primes that multiply to make it, like 12 = 2 times 2 times 3.

levels.a: Reads the prime factors from a factor tree, a diagram that splits a number into branches.
levels.b: Divides by primes, smallest first, until reaching 1.
levels.c: Writes a repeated prime with a small raised number (a power), so 3 times 3 times 3 is 3 cubed.
levels.d: Knows each number has only one prime breakdown, and spots one that isn't finished.
levels.e: Finds the smallest number to multiply by to get a square number, using the prime breakdown.
levels.f: Counts how many factors a number has, straight from its prime breakdown.

II.4.06.what: Finding the factors two numbers share, and the largest of these, called the greatest common factor (GCF).

levels.a: Lists all the factors of each number.
levels.b: Picks out the factors the two lists have in common.
levels.c: Finds the greatest common factor of two numbers.
levels.d: Finds the greatest common factor using the primes the two numbers share.

II.4.07.what: Putting the greatest common factor to work in fractions, packing problems and calculations.

levels.a: Simplifies a fraction by dividing top and bottom by their greatest common factor.
levels.b: Splits two kinds of items into identical packs with none left over.
levels.c: Rewrites a sum by pulling out the common factor, as in 12 + 15 = 3 times (4 + 5).
levels.d: Solves word problems, like cutting two ribbons into the longest equal pieces.

II.4.08.what: Finding the multiples two numbers share, and the smallest of these, called the least common multiple (LCM).

levels.a: Continues the list of multiples for each number.
levels.b: Picks out the multiples the two lists have in common.
levels.c: Finds the least common multiple of two numbers.
levels.d: Finds the least common multiple using prime breakdowns.

II.4.09.what: Putting the least common multiple to work in fractions and in problems about things lining up.

levels.a: Finds the smallest shared bottom number for two fractions.
levels.b: Works out when two repeating events next happen together, like two flashing lights.
levels.c: Solves word problems, like the smallest class that splits evenly into teams of 7 or 9.
levels.d: Uses the fact that the GCF times the LCM equals the two numbers multiplied together.
levels.e: Finds the least common multiple of three numbers, as in three lights flashing together.
levels.f: Counts numbers in a range that are multiples of one number or another, without counting twice.

II.4.10.what: Understanding square numbers, made by multiplying a number by itself, and why they are called squares.

levels.a: Sees a square number as dots arranged in a square.
levels.b: Knows the square numbers up to 12 times 12.
levels.c: Explains why square numbers have an odd number of factors: one factor pairs with itself.
levels.d: Spots patterns, like the gaps between squares going up by odd numbers.

II.4.11.what: Knowing whether a sum or product will be even or odd without working it out, and why.

levels.a: Predicts whether a sum is even or odd.
levels.b: Predicts whether a product is even or odd.
levels.c: Decides if a long sum or product is even or odd, for example by counting the odd numbers.
levels.d: Solves puzzles, like whether six odd numbers can add up to 35.

II.4.12.what: Solving puzzles and games that use factors and multiples.

levels.a: Solves mystery-number riddles from clues about factors.
levels.b: Adds up a number's factors to test for perfect numbers, like 6 = 1 + 2 + 3.
levels.c: Plays a factor game, working out which factors a partner scores.
levels.d: Explains a winning strategy, like why picking a large prime is a good first move.
levels.e: Finds a mystery number from three or more clues, including how many factors it has.
levels.f: Finds two numbers from their sum and product, by checking factor pairs.
